cards.literal_source: The body was involved in surviving what happened to you, and it has its own innate resolution process. Peter Levine, the founder of Somatic Experiencing therapy, in his book, [In An Unspoken Voice](https://www.amazon.com/Unspoken-Voice-Releases-Restores-Goodness/dp/1556439431), explains that his accidental realization about the need to release bodily trauma was corroborated by a park biologist in Malawi. He told Levine that captured animals who hadn’t trembled and breathed spontaneously before being released were unlikely to survive in the wild.

cards.literal_source:
But discovering the body’s programming isn’t simply something you can read a book for. Some bodies are frozen and need to shake. Some are dissociated and need to feel, cry, laugh, self-massage, breathe more, less, in new ways, etc. Learning to feel the body, connect with it, and let the energy flow the way it needs to, is like learning to ride a bike. You can read about it and follow the practices, and even pay lots of money to a Bike Expert, but ultimately, you have to feel it out and see what works.
Still, I do find that lasting complex trauma recovery tends to follow a general, kind of obvious sequence: 
Stay present so you can stay with what happens and choose what comes next.
Regulate or discharge accumulated activation energy
Work with trauma feelings before the story comes in
Work with memories you can actually point to: the actual events and the triggering events
Integrate, differentiate, and build a life of meaning. Decide your boundaries, direction, relationships, and overall identity.
Because specific somatic therapies are on a spectrum of physical<->emotional (or conscious<->subconscious), as well as a spectrum of intensity and specificity, we can often guess which one might be right for someone at which time. These don’t all have the same level or type of evidence supporting them, and there’s definitely no scientific roadmap that could survive peer review, but ultimately everyone somehow builds their own map of what makes sense, and this is mine. 
I use these therapies partly to make the body safer to inhabit before going into deeper [inner-child therapy](http://innerchild.u-dont-exist.com), where we intentionally re-expose ourselves to traumatic memories in an effort to re-parent the little one-one inside who was hurt.

cards.selection_condition: Use when genuine variation makes a fixed prescription inadequate; do not invent an analogy solely to fill a slot.

cards.literal_source: Currently, as a PTSD or cPTSD patient, your health insurance (if you're lucky enough to have it) might cover the most scientifically validated trauma therapies: Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing (EMDR) and trauma-focused Cognitive Behavioral Therapies.

cards.literal_source: All of these focus on the trauma memory itself, reactivating it in order to change the meaning and/or the processing and response to it. Their logic is simple: slowly increase your exposure to painful memories until you can fully re-live the experience without overwhelming your nervous system. The CBT trauma therapies also use regular CBT to re-narrate the meaning of the experiences, so that, for example, being abused as a child no longer creates a story that "I deserve abuse."
cards.sentence_clause_annotation: Three sentences remain on what the approaches do. The last is an instance of the same mechanism, not a new semantic obligation.
cards.selection_condition: Use to unpack a mechanism with a source-backed instance; do not generate an anecdote to satisfy the last node.

cards.literal_source:
Those therapies do show meaningful impact for many people in terms of reducing hyperarousal, and sometimes dissociation. But there are two main problems with them that
Peter Levine, et al. have [explained](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2015.00093/full). On the one hand, as Levine points out, exposure desensitization therapy can itself be re-traumatizing, which isn't well-captured in the positive evidence, because reasons for dropout and adverse events were often poorly or inconsistently reported. On the other hand, even when these trauma-memory approaches "work," they are working against the body's understanding of things by creating new cognitive-behavioral patterns that suppress the old conditioned fear responses as they come up. That can produce a reduction of symptoms without solving the root of them.
cards.symbolic_relation_map: CONCESSION > LIVE-OBJECTIONS{A[cause + evidence-limit], B[apparent success + remaining mechanism]} > CONSEQUENCE
cards.sentence_clause_annotation: The benefit receives less space than the two different objections. Each objection develops internally; they are not mirrored mini-essays.
cards.selection_condition: Use where real benefits coexist with unequal unresolved problems. The target decides number/length of complications.

cards.literal_source:
The philosophy behind somatic therapies starts from the other end. It assumes that the body actually knows how to release the tension it has stored. Instead of treating dissociation and hyperarousal as symptom endpoints to reduce, they use them to diagnose the structure of nervous system dysregulation. In Levine's SIBAM model (from Unspoken Voice), we can understand how dissociation and hyperarousal actually work by splitting up our ordinary holistic experience into five layers. Dissociation is when these layers are not well-connected. Hyperarousal is when channels are so tightly linked that one rapidly activates the others:
Sensation: feelings inside the body, like tension, balance, heat, etc.
Image: what you see, remember, dream
Behavior: voluntary, involuntary, and crucially, actions that got aborted mid-stream during the traumatic incident.
Affect: emotions, like fear, anger, grief, disgust, and joy. Also bodily feelings like vulnerability, hyper-vigilant panic, or profound relief.
Meaning: the story that explains all of these, containing beliefs and judgements.

cards.literal_source: Levine and many other somatic theorists believe that once the body can fully feel itself and unleash the energy that got stuck, the meaning layer that CBT addresses often handles itself. EMDR also works at the bodily level and allows the meaning level to handle itself, but it uses the body more as a barometer and metabolizer of distress encoded in memory networks rather than as the primary instrument of finishing the action that got blocked by trauma.

cards.literal_source: As I post this article today (Dec. 9, 2025), one of my best lifelong friends just had her father pass away from cancer (and other comorbidities) while she was meditating with him. Life and death are both sacred processes. I wish him an easy transition to his next life, and I pray his daughter will take his passing well.

cards.literal_source: Interestingly, she discovered a remedy that almost nobody knows about, but after she discovered it, she totally forgot about it! One day, she was in so much hip pain that she could not rest on the bed, as the cancer had spread to her bones. So, she started talking to her hip, sending it love and healing, and as she was doing that, her whole body melted into infinite cosmic orgasms, which is probably the most powerful spiritual peak experience she ever had in her life. I’ve also had other friends who had incredible peak spiritual experiences (while sober) but totally forgot about them. It’s quite an interesting phenomenon!

cards.literal_source: Anyway, treating cancer has been a topic that I’ve been researching for over a decade now, thanks to my mom, and so I thought I should write this article since people sometimes do ask what I would recommend. In writing the article, I really underestimated the amount of time it would take — there are people who dedicate their whole lives to writing on this subject— but I’ve done extensive additional research, which taught me that some treatments are not as effective as I thought (like GcMAF), and exposed me to a vast array that I never heard of before. If you have any treatment you’d like me to research, leave a comment and I will do my best.
